proposals.relationship: Benton explicitly credits Curtin’s world-history training as the foundation for Law and Colonial Cultures and acknowledges his example and continuing mentorship.
proposals.evidence_note: Own acknowledgmentsxi recounts Curtin repeatedly urging world rather than narrower Iberian, West African or Atlantic history and states the subsequent training provided the foundation for the later book. This is specific methodological formation, not merely institutional overlap; no claim that Curtin supplied every legal argument or that Benton’s scholarly detours were irrelevant.

proposals.relationship: Benton explicitly follows Braudel’s long-century convention to mark continuities that cross ordinary century boundaries in A Search for Sovereignty.
proposals.evidence_note: Own4/n5 states this precise adoption and explains varying chronological ranges. Narrow methodological resource only: no assertion of general Annales allegiance, derivation of all legal geography from Braudel, or an independently checked reading of Braudel’s original work.

proposals.relationship: Benton names Armitage among the scholars whose work she builds on to complicate conventional accounts of international law, using his analysis of natural and positive law together in the late eighteenth century.
proposals.evidence_note: Own6/n10 explicitly credits Armitage alongside Anghie, Keene and Sylvest rather than giving him exclusive credit;6/n11 specifies Declaration of Independence chapter2 as the particular resource.5/n8also quotes his imperium/dominium dilemma;acknowledgmentsxivcredit a Kingsbury/Armitage-convened group with shaping early ideas. Resource is substantive, not based solely on coattendance. Armitage’s books and other named originals unread here.

proposals.relationship: Benton draws on Cooper’s account of the uneven distribution of power and economic relations to frame the lumpiness of imperial formations and the possibilities for rewriting global history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own8/n14explicitly extends this insight chronologically/methodologically with Cooper’s Globalization essay101;7/n13uses Cooper’s uneven sovereignty discussion as a qualification to territorial narratives. Acknowledgmentsxivcredit Burbank and Cooper jointly for sharing ideas on imperial political imagination, not Cooper alone. Cited original essay/book unread; no claim Cooper originated all of Benton’s spatial argument.

proposals.relationship: Benton challenges Agamben’s model of exception by arguing that imperial suspensions of law often substituted or reconfigured legal authorization within layered sovereignty rather than producing an absence of law.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Humanity82–83answer explicitly makes this argument through martial law, penal colonies and bare sovereignty. Her account explains how law could sanction violence and does not equate legality with protection. Edelstein’s distinct81claims are not attributed to her. Her final83answer limits direct present-day equivalence and recognizes nineteenth-century changes. Agamben’s originals and Benton’s concluding book chapter remain unread; this is Benton’s specific historical objection, not proof that his entire theory is refuted.

proposals.relationship: Benton argues that world-systems accounts centered on economic primacy or Europe–Americas connections can miss the institutional and legal interconnections joining regions, proposing institutional world history as an alternative.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2002intro4/n5and6–7/nn9–10 explicitly critiques named variants and Asian-centered inversions as well as Eurocentric approaches. This is scoped criticism of those analytical frameworks, not rejection of every dependency argument or attribution of all cited positions to Wallerstein. Abu-Lughod, Voll and Frank retain their distinct cited roles and are absent person endpoints; no automatic personal Wallerstein arrow.
